claim: The static magnetic field of MRI scanners can induce a magneto-hydrodynamic stimulation of the vestibular organ (MVS).
source: The static magnetic field of MRI scanners can induce a magneto-hydrodynamic stimulation of the vestibular organ (MVS).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior research throughout the manuscript.

claim: In common fMRI settings, MVS leads to a vestibular ocular reflex (VOR).
source: In common fMRI settings, this MVS effect leads to a vestibular ocular reflex (VOR).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: All 17 healthy volunteers exhibited a rightward VOR inside the MRI-scanner as compared to outside-MRI conditions.
source: We investigated 17 healthy volunteers, all of which exhibited a rightward VOR inside the MRI-scanner as compared to outside-MRI conditions.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the results.

claim: When probing the distribution of overt spatial attention inside the MRI using a visual search task, subjects scanned a region of space that was significantly shifted toward the right.
source: More importantly, when probing the distribution of overt spatial attention inside the MRI using a visual search task, subjects scanned a region of space that was significantly shifted toward the right.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: An estimate of subjective straight-ahead orientation exhibited a rightward shift inside the MRI scanner.
source: An additional estimate of subjective straight-ahead orientation likewise exhibited a rightward shift.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Putting subjects in a 3T MRI-scanner elicits MVS-induced horizontal biases of spatial orienting and exploration, which closely mimic that of stroke patients with spatial neglect.
source: Hence, putting subjects in a 3T MRI-scanner elicits MVS-induced horizontal biases of spatial orienting and exploration, which closely mimic that of stroke patients with spatial neglect.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data and comparison to known neglect symptoms.

claim: Roberts et al., 2011 observed that healthy subjects exposed to the static magnetic field of 3T and 7T MRI scanners developed a persistent horizontal nystagmus in complete darkness.
source: Roberts et al., 2011 observed that healthy subjects who were exposed to the static magnetic field of 3T and 7T MRI scanners developed a persistent horizontal nystagmus in complete darkness.
evidence: This is a citation to prior research by Roberts et al., 2011.

claim: The MVS-induced nystagmus effect has been replicated by various groups.
source: Since then, this effect was replicated by various groups (e.g. Mian et al., 2013; Boegle et al., 2016) and was shown to be present for standard fMRI settings at 1.5T and 3T (Boegle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The nystagmus is caused by Lorentz forces that result from the interaction of the static magnetic field of the scanner and ionic currents in the endolymph fluid of the subject's labyrinth.
source: Moreover, these studies have further corroborated the initial conclusion by Roberts et al., 2011 that the nystagmus is caused by Lorentz forces that result from the interaction of the static magnetic field of the scanner and ionic currents in the endolymph fluid of the subject's labyrinth (see Ward et al., 2019 for review).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Lorentz force acts upon the cupulae of the horizontal and anterior semicircular canals, inducing a mixed horizontal and torsional nystagmus.
source: This force acts upon the cupulae of the horizontal and anterior semicircular canals, inducing a mixed horizontal and torsional nystagmus (Otero-Millan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Otero-Millan et al., 2017.

claim: The stronger horizontal component of the nystagmus comprises of a slow horizontal vestibular ocular reflex (VOR) that is accompanied by fast resetting saccades in the opposite direction.
source: The stronger horizontal component comprises of a slow horizontal vestibular ocular reflex (VOR) that is accompanied by fast resetting saccades in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the nystagmus pattern and is supported by established knowledge of VOR.

claim: In natural settings, a stimulation of the horizontal canals occurs when our head is accelerated to the left or to the right.
source: In natural settings, a stimulation of the horizontal canals occurs, for instance, when our head is accelerated to the left or to the right.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vestibular function.

claim: The VOR smoothly moves our eyes in the direction opposite to the head rotation.
source: The resulting VOR then smoothly moves our eyes in the direction opposite to the head rotation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VOR function.

claim: The VOR supports the stabilization of the retinal image despite head-motion, together with the visually induced optokinetic reflex.
source: The VOR thus supports – together with the visually induced optokinetic reflex – the stabilization of the retinal image despite head-motion (for review e.g. see Ilg, 1997; Angelaki and Cullen, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by review citations.

claim: MVS carries important ramifications and caveats for functional MRI studies of the vestibular system, cognition, motor control, and perception in general.
source: Roberts et al., 2011 (p.1638) pointed out that the fake head-motion signal induced by magneto-hydrodynamic vestibular stimulation (MVS) 'carries important ramifications and caveats for functional MRI studies, not only of the vestibular system but of cognition, motor control, and perception in general'.
evidence: This is a direct quote from Roberts et al., 2011.

claim: Boegle et al., 2016 observed that MVS modulates fMRI-signal fluctuations.
source: For instance, Boegle et al., 2016 observed that MVS does indeed modulate fMRI-signal fluctuations.
evidence: This is a citation to prior research by Boegle et al., 2016.

claim: MVS modulation affected the default mode network as a function of the strength of the magnetic field and mainly in areas associated with vestibular and oculomotor function.
source: This modulation affected the default mode network as a function of the strength of the magnetic field and mainly in areas associated with vestibular and oculomotor function.
evidence: This is based on findings from Boegle et al., 2016.

claim: MVS induces balance shifts in resting-state network dynamics that might be like a 'special patient group with a vestibular imbalance' but without lesions in the inner ear or central nervous system.
source: Thus, MVS induces balance shifts in resting-state network dynamics that might be 'like a "special patient group with a vestibular imbalance" but without lesions in the inner ear or central nervous system' (Boegle et al., 2016; p.420).
evidence: This is a direct quote from Boegle et al., 2016.

claim: In healthy subjects, caloric vestibular stimulation (CVS) of one external auditory canal induces a VOR and provokes 'neglect-like' behavioral phenomena.
source: For example, in healthy subjects, caloric vestibular stimulation (CVS) of one external auditory canal not only induces a VOR but also provokes 'neglect-like' behavioral phenomena.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CVS effects.

claim: Stroke patients with spatial neglect show a tonic deviation of head and eyes towards the ipsilesional side.
source: Stroke patients with spatial neglect show a tonic deviation of head and eyes towards the ipsilesional side and no longer explore or orient towards large parts of space contralateral to their lesion and therefore neglect contralesionally located people or objects (Heilman et al., 1983; Karnath, 2015, for a review).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Stroke patients with spatial neglect no longer explore or orient towards large parts of space contralateral to their lesion and therefore neglect contralesionally located people or objects.
source: Stroke patients with spatial neglect show a tonic deviation of head and eyes towards the ipsilesional side and no longer explore or orient towards large parts of space contralateral to their lesion and therefore neglect contralesionally located people or objects (Heilman et al., 1983; Karnath, 2015, for a review).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In healthy volunteers, CVS induces a tonic bias of head orientation around the yaw axis.
source: In healthy volunteers, CVS induces a tonic bias of head orientation around the yaw axis (Karnath et al., 2003) and a tonic shift of the average horizontal eye position (Abderhalden, 1926; Jung, 1953).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CVS induces a tonic shift of the average horizontal eye position in healthy volunteers.
source: In healthy volunteers, CVS induces a tonic bias of head orientation around the yaw axis (Karnath et al., 2003) and a tonic shift of the average horizontal eye position (Abderhalden, 1926; Jung, 1953).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CVS-induced orientation biases resemble those observed in neurological patients suffering from spatial neglect.
source: Both of these orientation biases resemble those observed in neurological patients suffering from spatial neglect (cf. Fruhmann-Berger and Karnath, 2005): already at rest, that is when doing nothing, these patients' head and eyes are tonically deviated towards the ipsilesional side.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: CVS in darkness induces a bias in subjective straight-ahead (SSA) in healthy subjects, mimicking the bias of the SSA in neglect patients towards their ipsilesional side.
source: Moreover, CVS in darkness even induces a bias in subjective straight-ahead (SSA) in healthy subjects, mimicking the bias of the SSA in neglect patients towards their ipsilesional side (e.g. Karnath et al., 1994c; Chokron and Imbert, 1995; Kapoor et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CVS biases healthy subjects' scan path during visual search.
source: Finally, CVS biases healthy subjects' scan path during visual search (Karnath et al., 1996): when exploring their surroundings for possible targets subjects' eye movements are no longer symmetrically distributed in the horizontal dimension but biased towards one side of the body's midsaggital plane.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: When exploring their surroundings for possible targets during CVS, subjects' eye movements are no longer symmetrically distributed in the horizontal dimension but biased towards one side of the body's midsaggital plane.
source: Finally, CVS biases healthy subjects' scan path during visual search (Karnath et al., 1996): when exploring their surroundings for possible targets subjects' eye movements are no longer symmetrically distributed in the horizontal dimension but biased towards one side of the body's midsaggital plane.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The CVS-induced horizontal bias in spatial attention is resembled by the spontaneous, asymmetrical, spatially biased exploratory behavior of neglect patients.
source: Also this CVS-induced horizontal bias in spatial attention is resembled by the spontaneous, asymmetrical, spatially biased exploratory behavior of neglect patients (Karnath et al., 1996; Karnath et al., 1998), leading to 'spatial neglect' of one side of the surrounding scene.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It is possible to compensate the spontaneous biases of neglect patients through CVS.
source: Conversely, it is possible to compensate the spontaneous biases of neglect patients through CVS (Rubens, 1985; Karnath, 1994b; Vallar et al., 1995; Karnath et al., 1996; Rode et al., 1998; for review e.g. see Rossetti and Rode, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MVS should induce a horizontal bias in both the exploratory scan path during visual search and in the SSA of healthy subjects, resembling the horizontal biases of neglect patients.
source: We hypothesized that MVS should induce a horizontal bias in both the exploratory scan path during visual search and in the SSA of healthy subjects, resembling the horizontal biases of neglect patients.
evidence: This is the stated hypothesis of the study.

claim: The study analyzed oculomotor behavior of 17 healthy subjects inside and outside a standard 3T MRI scanner (Siemens MAGNETOM Prisma).
source: To address our research question we analyzed oculomotor behavior of 17 healthy subjects inside and outside a standard 3T MRI scanner (Siemens MAGNETOM Prisma).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: All subjects provided their informed consent according to the guidelines of the institutional ethics board.
source: All subjects provided their informed consent according to the guidelines of our institutional ethics board.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical procedures.

claim: The strength of the magnetic field at the outside position (~125 cm horizontal displacement) is roughly 10 times smaller than at the scanner center.
source: an initial 'outside 1' phase with our subjects on the scanner-table at its maximal horizontal displacement from the scanner center (head coil at ~125 cm horizontal [0 cm vertical] displacement); the strength of the magnetic field in this position is roughly 10 times smaller than at the scanner center (compare Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by reference to a figure.

claim: The strength of the uniform magnetic field at the scanner center is 3 Tesla.
source: a subsequent 'inside' phase with the subject's head being in the center of the scanner bore where the strength of the uniform magnetic field is 3 Tesla
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the experimental setup.

claim: During the inside phase, the typical saw-tooth-like eye movement pattern characteristic for a vestibular nystagmus was observed in the exemplary subject.
source: Figure 1 illustrates the resulting eye-data of an exemplary subject throughout all tasks and phases. It shows that during the inside phase the typical saw-tooth-like eye movement pattern, which is characteristic for a vestibular nystagmus, was observed (also compare Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: The nystagmus consisted of a slow rightward VOR that was accompanied by fast resetting saccades in the opposite leftward direction.
source: It consisted of a slow rightward VOR that was accompanied by fast resetting saccades in the opposite leftward direction.
evidence: This describes the observed nystagmus pattern.

claim: The prototypical nystagmus-pattern was largely reduced for the outside 1 phase and was practically absent for the outside 2 phase.
source: This prototypical nystagmus-pattern was largely reduced for the outside 1 phase and it was practically absent for the outside 2 phase.
evidence: This describes the observed pattern across experimental phases.

claim: The average slow eye velocity for the outside 1 phase was 0.30°/s (± 0.49°/s SD).
source: The average slow eye velocity for the outside 1 phase was 0.30°/s on average ( ± 0.49°/s standard deviation [SD]) and increased to 1.42°/s ( ± 1.49°/s SD) for the inside phase.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: The average slow eye velocity increased to 1.42°/s (± 1.49°/s SD) for the inside phase.
source: The average slow eye velocity for the outside 1 phase was 0.30°/s on average ( ± 0.49°/s standard deviation [SD]) and increased to 1.42°/s ( ± 1.49°/s SD) for the inside phase.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: After removing the subjects from the scanner bore to outside 2, average slow eye velocity decreased to –0.01°/s (± 0.40°/s SD).
source: After removing the subjects from the scanner bore to outside 2, average slow eye velocity decreased to –0.01°/s ( ± 0.40°/s SD).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: The within-subject differences in velocity between outside 1 and inside were significant (t(16)=6.62, p < 0.001, g1[CI95%] = 1.60 [0.87, 2.32]).
source: The within-subject differences in velocity between outside 1 and inside and between inside and outside 2 were significant (one-tailed paired t-test: t(16)=6.62, p < 0.001, g1[CI95%] = 1.60 [0.87, 2.32] and t(16)=6.69, p < 0.001, g1[CI95%] = 1.62 [0.88, 2.35], respectively).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The within-subject differences in velocity between inside and outside 2 were significant (t(16)=6.69, p < 0.001, g1[CI95%] = 1.62 [0.88, 2.35]).
source: The within-subject differences in velocity between outside 1 and inside and between inside and outside 2 were significant (one-tailed paired t-test: t(16)=6.62, p < 0.001, g1[CI95%] = 1.60 [0.87, 2.32] and t(16)=6.69, p < 0.001, g1[CI95%] = 1.62 [0.88, 2.35], respectively).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Average horizontal eye velocity during outside 1 was slightly larger as compared to outside 2 (t(16)=3.08, p = 0.007, g1[CI95%] = 0.75 [0.20, 1.28]).
source: Average horizontal eye velocity during outside 1 was also slightly larger as compared to outside 2 (two-tailed paired t-test: t(16)=3.08, p = 0.007, g1[CI95%] = 0.75 [0.20, 1.28]).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The MVS effects affected only horizontal eye movements and were absent in the vertical direction.
source: As expected (Otero-Millan et al., 2017), the MVS effects affected only horizontal eye movements of our 2D eye movement recordings and were absent in the vertical direction (outside 1: –0.29°/s ± 0.56°/s SD; inside: –0.29°/s ± 0.60°/s SD; outside 2: –0.21°/s ± 0.58°/s SD; statistical comparisons with two-tailed paired t-tests yielded no significant differences in vertical eye velocity between any of the three task phases [p > 0.20]).
evidence: This is experimental data and statistical analysis, with citation to prior expectation.

claim: The horizontal bias in the exemplary subject's exploratory eye movements was reflected by the distribution of overt attention, that is the endpoints of the saccades guiding visual search.
source: This horizontal bias in our subject's exploratory eye movements was not a mere consequence of the rightward VOR inside the scanner but was likewise reflected by the distribution of overt attention, that is the endpoints of the saccades guiding visual search
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The mean horizontal position of saccade endpoints almost perfectly resembled the center of the search screen for the outside 1 and 2 phases, while it was clearly shifted to the right for the inside phase.
source: the mean horizontal position of these saccade endpoints (indicated by the blue vertical lines in the rightmost plots in Figure 1) almost perfectly resembled the center of the search screen for the outside 1 and 2 phases, while it was clearly shifted to the right for the inside phase.
evidence: This describes data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The average horizontal mean of visual search was at 1.65° (± 4.40° SD) for the outside 1 phase.
source: Across our 17 subjects, statistical analysis of subjects' exploratory spatial behavior (Figure 3) revealed that the average horizontal mean of visual search was at 1.65° ( ± 4.40° SD) and at 1.01° ( ± 3.98° SD) for the outside 1 and 2 phases, respectively, while inside this measure was significantly shifted to 4.69° ( ± 4.61°) towards the right
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: The average horizontal mean of visual search was at 1.01° (± 3.98° SD) for the outside 2 phase.
source: Across our 17 subjects, statistical analysis of subjects' exploratory spatial behavior (Figure 3) revealed that the average horizontal mean of visual search was at 1.65° ( ± 4.40° SD) and at 1.01° ( ± 3.98° SD) for the outside 1 and 2 phases, respectively, while inside this measure was significantly shifted to 4.69° ( ± 4.61°) towards the right
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: Inside the scanner, the horizontal mean of visual search was significantly shifted to 4.69° (± 4.61°) towards the right.
source: Across our 17 subjects, statistical analysis of subjects' exploratory spatial behavior (Figure 3) revealed that the average horizontal mean of visual search was at 1.65° ( ± 4.40° SD) and at 1.01° ( ± 3.98° SD) for the outside 1 and 2 phases, respectively, while inside this measure was significantly shifted to 4.69° ( ± 4.61°) towards the right (one-tailed paired t-tests; outside 1 vs. inside: t(16)=-5.12, p < 0.001, g1[CI95%] = 1.24 [0.59, 1.87]; inside vs. outside 2: t(16)=4.38, p < 0.001, g1[CI95%] = 1.06 [0.45, 1.65]).
evidence: This is experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The horizontal mean of visual search did not significantly differ between phases outside 1 and 2 (t(16)=0.76, p = 0.46, g1[CI95%] = −0.18 [-0.66, 0.30]).
source: The measures did not significantly differ between phases outside 1 and 2 (two-tailed paired t-test: t(16)=0.76, p = 0.46, g1[CI95%] = −0.18 [-0.66, 0.30]).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The SSA exhibited a significant rightward shift from the outside 1 (1.79° ± 5.39° SD) to the inside (4.76° ± 4.02° SD) phase (t(16)=-2.38, p = 0.015, g1[CI95%] = 0.58 [0.05, 1.08]).
source: Across our 17 subjects, the SSA likewise exhibited a significant rightward shift from the outside 1 (1.79° ± 5.39° SD) to the inside (4.76° ± 4.02° SD) phase (one-tailed paired t-test: t(16)=-2.38, p = 0.015, g1[CI95%] = 0.58 [0.05, 1.08]; compare Figure 4).
evidence: This is experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The SSA effect vanished after removing subjects from the scanner in the outside 2 phase (0.26° ± 4.37° SD; t(16)=3.56, p = 0.001, g1[CI95%] = 0.86 [0.29, 1.42]).
source: This effect vanished after removing subjects from the scanner in the outside 2 phase (0.26° ± 4.37° SD; one-tailed paired t-test: t(16)=3.56, p = 0.001, g1[CI95%] = 0.86 [0.29, 1.42]).
evidence: This is experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference between the SSA for phases outside 1 and 2 (t(16)=1.17, p = 0.26, g1[CI95%] = −0.28 [-0.76, 0.21]).
source: There was no significant difference between the SSA for phases outside 1 and 2 (two-tailed paired t-test: t(16)=1.17, p = 0.26, g1[CI95%] = −0.28 [-0.76, 0.21]).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The MVS-effect is inverted when subject-positioning is reversed with respect to the static magnetic field vector of the MRI-scanner.
source: The rationale behind this manipulation was that the MVS-effect is inverted when subject-positioning is reversed with respect to the static magnetic field vector of the MRI-scanner (e.g. compare Roberts et al., 2011), while there is no change in alertness or arousal as compared to our main experiment.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In the 'feet first' control experiment, subjects exhibited a strong leftward VOR inside the scanner (–1.48°/s ± 1.43°/s SD) as compared to both outside 1 and 2 phases (0.36°/s ± 0.30°/s SD & 0.49°/s ± 0.24°/s SD).
source: In brief, subjects now exhibited a strong leftward VOR inside the scanner (–1.48°/s ± 1.43°/s SD) as compared to both outside 1 and 2 phases (0.36°/s ± 0.30°/s SD & 0.49°/s ± 0.24°/s SD) (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from the control experiment.

claim: In the 'feet first' control experiment, the biases in overt spatial attention and the perception of SSA reversed to the left side.
source: Importantly, the biases in overt spatial attention (outside 1: 1.12° ± 3.39° SD; inside: –2.82° ± 4.57° SD; outside 2: 2.06° ± 2.05° SD; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and the perception of SSA (outside 1: 2.74° ± 2.76° SD; inside: –4.97° ± 3.49° SD; outside 2: 1.70° ± 1.46° SD; see Figure 4—figure supplement 1) reversed as well.
evidence: This is experimental data from the control experiment.

claim: The spatial biases in the 'feet first' control experiment were toward the left side and thus in the direction predicted by MVS.
source: In other words, the spatial biases were now toward the left side and thus in the direction predicted by MVS.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the control experiment results.

claim: The average change in VOR velocity for the inside phase as compared to both outside 1 and 2 phases reliably predicted respective changes in both visual search (R² = 0.53; F(1,21)=23.43; p < 0.001) and in subjects' SSA (R² = 0.46; F(1,21)=18.04; p < 0.001).
source: Indeed, the average change in VOR velocity for the inside phase as compared to both outside 1 and 2 phases reliably predicted respective changes in both visual search (R² = 0.53; F(1,21)=23.43; p < 0.001) and in subjects' SSA (R² = 0.46; F(1,21)=18.04; p < 0.001) (also compare Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of the relationship between VOR and behavioral measures.

claim: The VOR velocity inside the MRT amounted to 1.42°/s during the looking straight-ahead task.
source: The velocity of the VOR inside the MRT amounted to 1.42°/s during our looking straight-ahead task.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: The task instruction to 'fixate an imaginary target' probably reduced VOR-velocity by about 25% as compared to a situation without such imaginary fixation.
source: Our task instruction to 'fixate an imaginary target', namely into the direction of a previously illuminated target LED in the medial plane, probably reduced VOR-velocity by about 25% as compared to a situation without such imaginary fixation (cf. Schmäl et al., 2000; Barr et al., 1976).
evidence: This is an inference based on citations to prior research.

claim: The VOR estimate of 1.42°/s corresponds to the roughly 2°/s VOR reported in an earlier MVS study at 3T without imaginary fixation.
source: Given this latter consideration, our estimate well corresponds to the roughly 2°/s VOR reported in an earlier MVS study, which used a comparable experimental setting at 3T but without imaginary fixation (Boegle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research findings.

claim: Lying inside the 3T MRI scanner led to a spatially biased neglect-like behavior when subjects were trying to look straight ahead and when they were performing visual search.
source: Our experiment further revealed that lying inside the 3T MRI scanner (in the common position in neurology/neuroscience, i.e. with head first) also led to a spatially biased neglect-like behavior when subjects were trying to look straight ahead and when they were performing visual search.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: The biases in the looking straight ahead task and the visual search task were not a mere reflection of the tonic VOR-induced drift of subjects' eyes toward the right.
source: First of all, we would like to point out that the respective biases in the looking straight ahead task and the visual search task were not a mere reflection of the tonic VOR-induced drift of subjects' eyes toward the right.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The critical behavioral measure in both tasks refers to the distribution of endpoints of subjects' voluntary saccades while they were trying to follow task instructions.
source: The critical behavioral measure in both tasks refers to the distribution of endpoints of subjects' voluntary saccades while they were trying to follow task instructions.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the behavioral measure used.

claim: The passive drift of subjects' eyes due to the MVS-induced VOR does not influence the measure of active spatial behavior.
source: The passive drift of subjects' eyes due to the MVS-induced VOR does not influence this measure of active spatial behavior (for further discussion also cf. Karnath et al., 1996, p.340).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: In the visual search task, the center of subjects' visual scan-path was shifted by roughly 3.4° to the right inside the scanner.
source: Hence, the reported shifts inside the scanner reflect a true spatial bias in overt spatial attention and active goal-directed behavior: (i) in the visual search task the center of subjects' visual scan-path (in the absence of any visible target) was shifted by roughly 3.4° to the right
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data.

claim: In the looking straight ahead task, the average endpoint of subjects' saccades in darkness deviated toward the right by about 3.7°.
source: (ii) in the looking straight ahead task, the average endpoint of subjects' saccades in darkness likewise deviated toward the right, namely by about 3.7°.
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data.

claim: The MVS-induced changes in VOR reliably predicted the changes in visual search and in the SSA across experiments.
source: The MVS-induced changes in VOR that we observed in our study did reliably predict the changes in visual search and in the SSA across experiments (compare Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on regression analysis of the data.

claim: There was a significant decrease of the residual rightward VOR from the outside 1 phase to the outside 2 phase.
source: Interestingly, we also revealed a significant decrease of the residual rightward VOR from the outside 1 phase to the outside 2 phase.
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: The decrease in VOR from the outside 1 phase to the outside 2 phase could be the result of a VOR set-point adaptation that has been shown to occur for longer exposure to MVS at 7T.
source: The decrease in VOR from the outside 1 phase to the outside 2 phase could be the result of a VOR set-point adaptation that has been shown to occur for longer exposure to MVS at 7T: in the presence of conflicting afferent inputs signaling spatial stability (such as from the otoliths etc.), the nervous system counteracts the MVS-induced tonic imbalance, as is obvious from a slow but incomplete reduction of the VOR over the course of minutes to hours (Jareonsettasin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation based on prior research findings.

claim: After CVS, healthy subjects' estimates about SSA, quantified by verbally instructing orientation of a laser-spot into this direction, shifted horizontally.
source: After CVS, healthy subjects' estimates about SSA, quantified by verbally instructing orientation of a laser-spot into this direction, shifted horizontally (e.g. Karnath et al., 1994c; Karnath et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CVS leads to a horizontal shift of healthy subjects' scan path during visual search.
source: Moreover, CVS likewise leads to a horizontal shift of healthy subjects' scan path during visual search (Karnath et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The known CVS-induced deviations ranged roughly between 4° and 9°.
source: These known CVS-induced deviations ranged roughly between 4° and 9° and thus were slightly larger than the MVS-induced spatial bias observed in the present experiment.
evidence: This is based on prior research findings.

claim: The CVS-induced biases in spatial behavior also surface when trying to manually point straight ahead and during manual spatial exploration.
source: Importantly, the CVS-induced biases in spatial behavior also surface when trying to manually point straight ahead (Schmäl et al., 2000) and during manual spatial exploration (Karnath et al., 2003), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CVS and probably also MVS induce changes in spatial representations for goal-directed actions that are effector-independent.
source: This suggests that CVS − and probably also MVS − does induce changes in spatial representations for goal-directed actions that are effector-independent.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior research and current findings.

claim: The CVS/MVS-induced alterations of spatial behavior are most likely of cerebro-cortical origin.
source: These CVS/MVS-induced alterations of spatial behavior are most likely of cerebro-cortical origin.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of vestibular processing.

claim: There exists no 'primary vestibular cortex' in the strict sense but rather an interconnected multimodal 'cortico-vestibular system' with the parieto-insular vestibular cortex (PIVC) at its core.
source: Notably, there exists no 'primary vestibular cortex' in the strict sense but rather an interconnected multimodal 'cortico-vestibular system' with the parieto-insular vestibular cortex (PIVC) at its core (e.g. see Guldin and Grüsser, 1998; Karnath and Dieterich, 2006; Lopez and Blanke, 2011 for reviews).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by review citations.

claim: The cortico-vestibular system includes neighboring parts in the temporo-parietal junction, posterior parietal cortex, superior temporal cortex, anterior insula, retroinsular regions, somatosensory cortex, cingulate cortex, premotor cortex, and hippocampus.
source: The areas that make up this system further entail neighboring parts in the temporo-parietal junction, posterior parietal cortex, superior temporal cortex, as well as regions in the anterior insula, retroinsular regions, somatosensory cortex, cingulate cortex, premotor cortex, and in the hippocampus (Guldin and Grüsser, 1998; Kahane et al., 2003; Karnath and Dieterich, 2006; Lopez et al., 2012; zu Eulenburg et al., 2012; Mazzola et al., 2014; Frank and Greenlee, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Neurons in part of these areas integrate vestibular cues (along with neck proprioception and information about eye position) in a way that allows them to represent visual action goals in reference to the body.
source: Neurons in part of these areas have been shown to integrate vestibular cues (along with neck proprioception and information about eye position) in a way that allows them to represent visual action goals in reference to the body (e.g. Andersen et al., 1999; Cohen and Andersen, 2002; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Body-centered, egocentric representation of spatial information underlies the guidance of goal-directed behavior including saccades, reaching, or heading.
source: This body-centered, egocentric representation of spatial information underlies, for example, the guidance of our goal-directed behavior including saccades, reaching, or heading etc. (see Karnath, 2001 for review).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a review citation.

claim: Body referencing has been reported in human functional imaging studies.
source: Such 'body referencing' has also been reported in human functional imaging studies (e.g. Bottini et al., 2001; Galati et al., 2010; Schindler and Bartels, 2013; Saj et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Tonic MVS (as well as CVS) introduces systematic biases in spatial action-representations, leading to alterations of subjective straight ahead and spatial exploration.
source: It thus is conceivable that tonic MVS (as well as CVS, etc.) introduces systematic biases in these spatial action-representations, leading to the reported alterations of subjective straight ahead and spatial exploration (also compare Laurens and Angelaki, 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and prior knowledge.

claim: Altered body referencing was suggested to explain the horizontal shifts in spatial behavior present in spatial neglect.
source: Similarly, altered body referencing was suggested to explain the horizontal shifts in spatial behavior present in spatial neglect (Karnath, 1994a; see Karnath, 2015 for a review).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The pattern of lesions exhibited by patients with spatial neglect is largely overlapping with the multimodal cortico-vestibular system and exhibits a common lateralization.
source: Moreover, the pattern of lesions exhibited by patients with spatial neglect is largely overlapping with the multimodal cortico-vestibular system and exhibits a common lateralization (Karnath and Dieterich, 2006; Karnath and Rorden, 2012; Dieterich and Brandt, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MVS induces neglect-like alterations of spatial behavior in healthy subjects and these alterations are supposedly due to its interference with the cortico-vestibular system, the same system that is typically affected in patients suffering from spatial neglect.
source: Hence, MVS induces neglect-like alterations of spatial behavior in healthy subjects and these alterations are supposedly due to its interference with the cortico-vestibular system, the same system that is typically affected in patients suffering from spatial neglect.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and prior knowledge.

claim: Healthy subjects exposed to the static magnetic field of an MR scanner developed a persistent horizontal nystagmus that slowly diminished but did not extinguish.
source: In this context, the observations that healthy subjects exposed to the static magnetic field of an MR scanner developed a persistent horizontal nystagmus that slowly diminished but did not extinguish (Roberts et al., 2011; Jareonsettasin et al., 2016), is highly interesting since the effect of, for example, CVS only lasts for several minutes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The effect of CVS only lasts for several minutes.
source: In this context, the observations that healthy subjects exposed to the static magnetic field of an MR scanner developed a persistent horizontal nystagmus that slowly diminished but did not extinguish (Roberts et al., 2011; Jareonsettasin et al., 2016), is highly interesting since the effect of, for example, CVS only lasts for several minutes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The tonic nature of MVS could serve as a noninvasive and comfortable means to continuously stimulate the labyrinth of neurological patients with spatial neglect and might help to induce longer-term plastic changes in patients' pathologically altered spatial representations.
source: If its effects on spatial exploration and orientation would follow a similar time-course, the tonic nature of MVS could serve as a noninvasive and comfortable means to continuously stimulate the labyrinth of neurological patients with spatial neglect and might help to induce longer-term plastic changes in patients' pathologically altered spatial representations (cf. Jareonsettasin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: The reported MVS effects on spatial orienting and attention are likely present during any fMRI study, at least at 3T.
source: Finally, we would like to emphasize that the reported MVS effects on spatial orienting and attention are likely present during any fMRI study, at least at 3T.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: It is very likely that MVS effects on spatial orienting and attention scale linearly with magnetic field strength, as is the case for the VOR.
source: Based on the present observation that the MVS-induced changes in VOR predicted the observed changes in visual search and SSA, it is very likely that these effects do scale linearly with magnetic field strength, as is the case for the VOR (e.g. Boegle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and prior research.

claim: Despite suppression of the VOR, vestibular information pertains in the central nervous system and can still exert its influence on spatial orienting and attention.
source: Yet, despite suppression of the VOR, we know that vestibular information pertains in the central nervous system (e.g. Buettner and Büttner, 1979; Angelaki and Cullen, 2008) and thus can still exert its influence on spatial orienting and attention.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When vestibular nystagmus is suppressed by fixating a small spot of light, there is little change in the maximal firing rate of single neurons recorded in the vestibular nuclei of monkeys: the activity in 80% of the neurons is reduced by only less than 10%.
source: For instance, when vestibular nystagmus is suppressed by fixating a small spot of light, there is little change in the maximal firing rate of single neurons recorded in the vestibular nuclei of monkeys: the activity in 80% of the neurons is reduced by only less than 10% (Buettner and Büttner, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Behavioral studies performed under regular lighting conditions have documented an influence of vestibular stimulation on spatial cognition.
source: In correspondence, behavioral studies performed under regular lighting conditions have documented an influence of vestibular stimulation on spatial cognition (see Ferrè and Haggard, 2020 for a review).
evidence: This is supported by a review citation.

claim: Boegle et al., 2016 showed that MVS had an impact on resting state activity in the default mode network and in particular in those areas related to vestibular and oculomotor function.
source: So far, they could show that MVS had an impact on resting state activity in the default mode network and in particular in those areas related to vestibular and oculomotor function.
evidence: This is a citation to prior research by Boegle et al., 2016.

claim: Boegle et al., 2017 demonstrated that MVS induces a modulation of visual-vestibular network activity.
source: In their follow-up work, these authors further demonstrated that MVS indeed did induce a modulation of visual-vestibular network activity (Boegle et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research by Boegle et al., 2017.

claim: Neural consequences of MVS should be critically considered in any fMRI study, together with MVS effects on spatial orienting, overt attention, and VOR.
source: Such neural consequences of MVS should – together with MVS effects on spatial orienting, overt attention, and VOR – be critically considered in any fMRI study.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Seventeen healthy subjects were recruited for the experiment (5 males; average age 25.1 ± 5.0 years SD).
source: We recruited seventeen healthy subjects for our experiment (5 males; average age 25.1 ± 5.0 years SD).
evidence: This describes the study sample.

claim: All subjects reported to be right-handed, had normal or corrected to normal vision, did not report any vestibular or neurological disease.
source: All subjects reported to be right-handed, had normal or corrected to normal vision, did not report any vestibular or neurological disease, and provided their informed consent according to our institutional ethics board guidelines prior to our experiment.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for the study.

claim: Sample size was guided by two separate power analyses (α = 0.025; power = 97.5%, each) informed by studies by Boegle et al., 2016 and Karnath et al., 1996.
source: Sample size was guided by two separate power analyses (α = 0.025; power = 97.5%, each) informed by the studies by Boegle et al., 2016 (3T MVS-induced VOR; data from their Figure 1a) and Karnath et al., 1996 (changes of SSA due to CVS and neck muscle vibration; data from their Table 1), respectively.
evidence: This describes the rationale for sample size determination.

claim: Both power analyses suggest a minimum sample size of 13 subjects.
source: Both analyses suggest a minimum sample size of 13 subjects (one-tailed one-sample/paired t-test).
evidence: This is the result of the power analyses.

claim: A 3T Siemens MAGNETOM Prisma MRI Scanner was used to apply MVS.
source: We used a 3T Siemens MAGNETOM Prisma MRI Scanner to apply MVS.
evidence: This describes the equipment used.

claim: No radio frequency (RF) or gradient coil fields were applied during the experiment.
source: No radio frequency (RF) or gradient coil fields were applied.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: Given standard subject positioning in neurology/neuroscience (subjects entering the scanner with their head first), the magnetic field vector of the MRI system pointed from subjects' toes to their head.
source: Given standard subject positioning in neurology/neuroscience (subjects entering the scanner with their head first), the magnetic field vector of our MRI system pointed from subjects' toes to their head.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: The magnetic field direction in the study is the exact opposite direction as compared to the situation in the study of Roberts et al., 2011.
source: Note that this is the exact opposite direction as compared to the situation in the study of Roberts et al., 2011.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research.

claim: The MVS-induced VOR effects should be towards the right and thus in the opposite horizontal direction as compared to Roberts et al., 2011.
source: Accordingly, the MVS-induced VOR effects should be towards the right and thus in the opposite horizontal direction as compared to theirs.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental setup and prior research.

claim: Subjects' head was positioned to tilt slightly backwards inside the head-coil to maximize the effects of MVS on the horizontal canals.
source: We tried to maximize the effects of MVS on the horizontal canals by positioning subjects in a way that their head would tilt slightly backwards inside the head-coil (Siemens Head/Neck 20 A 3T Tim Coil).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: According to Roberts et al., 2011 and Boegle et al., 2016, 'pitching-up' of subject's head can increase MVS-effects on the VOR.
source: According to the results reported by Roberts et al., 2011 and Boegle et al., 2016, such 'pitching-up' of subject's head can increase MVS-effects on the VOR.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A head pitch angle of about –30° (canthus-tragus-line vs. vertical) was approximated to consistently achieve strong MVS-effects in all subjects.
source: Based on these authors' results we approximated a head pitch angle of about –30° (canthus-tragus-line vs. vertical) to consistently achieve strong MVS-effects in all subjects.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup based on prior research.
